lead: Break a rule and you pay for it on the water, at once and unasked. Which penalty fits which breach, how to take it, and when turns are not enough.

sections.title: Which penalty for which breach

qa.q: How many penalty turns do I owe for a port-starboard foul under rule 44?
qa.a: Two: breaking a Part 2 rule (rules 10 to 23), such as port tack failing to keep clear, costs a **Two-Turns Penalty**, taken promptly whether or not anyone protests. Touching a mark costs one turn; both in one incident, two.

refs: RRS Part 2 preamble, RRS definition Racing

blocks.p: Break a rule without being exonerated and you take the penalty promptly, protest or no protest. For a rule of **Part 2** (rules 10 to 23) it is a **Two-Turns Penalty**; for touching a mark (rule 31), a **One-Turn Penalty**, even if swept there. Both in one incident: two turns.

tiles.name: Two-Turns Penalty
tiles.note: port tack fails to keep clear

blocks.p: Turns pay for these rules only: for rule 42 or 49 you retire, or the protest committee decides. Each incident, and each boat that may have broken a rule, needs its own penalty. If you broke none, a hail of "Protest" obliges you to nothing. Not yet racing, or finished and clear of the line: no turns owed. The sailing instructions may replace the turns with another penalty.

sections.title: Clear, prompt, the same way round

qa.q: How do I do penalty turns correctly, and which way do I turn?
qa.a: Get **well clear** of other boats soon after the incident, then turn promptly: each turn has one tack and one gybe, in either order, and both turns go the same way. While turning you keep clear of others.

blocks.p: Sail **well clear** of other boats as soon after the incident as you can, then turn **promptly**. Each turn includes one tack and one gybe, in either order; both turns go the same way. Two tacks are not a turn, and turns a leg later do not count.

fig.note: Downwind: gybe, luff, tack, bear away

blocks.p: While turning you **keep clear** of boats not taking a penalty (rule 21.2). If reasonably possible others must not interfere, but after the start a boat on her proper course need not avoid you (rule 23.2). A mark touched during the turns costs one more turn.

fig.note: Turns beyond the line: come back, cross again

blocks.p: A penalty earned before the start need not wait for the starting signal. At the **finish** your hull must be completely back on the course side after the turns before you cross the line; likewise after touching a finishing mark.

qa.q: When do I have to retire instead of doing penalty turns?
qa.a: When your breach caused **injury or serious damage**, or despite the turns gained you a significant advantage in the race or series. Then turns do not pay: you retire, or a hearing disqualifies you.

blocks.p: Turns do not pay if you caused **injury** or **serious damage**, or if despite them your breach gained you a **significant advantage** in the race or series: then you **retire**.

fig.note: A hole in Grey's side: retire, turns do not count

blocks.p: A retired boat scores boats entered plus one and must not hinder boats still racing. After a restart or resail, breaches in the first attempt go unpenalised, except rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 and rule 14 with injury or serious damage.

sections.title: A rule broken, no penalty owed

qa.q: Do I owe penalty turns if another boat forced me to break a rule?
qa.a: No: under **rule 43** you are exonerated when another boat's breach compelled you to break a rule, for example by pushing you onto a mark. An exonerated boat takes no penalty.

blocks.p: Rule 43 **exonerates** you when another boat's breach **compelled** you to break a rule; when, sailing within the **room or mark-room** owed to you, you broke a right-of-way rule or rule 15 or 16 against the boat that owed it, or were forced onto the mark (rule 31); and when, holding right of way, you broke rule 14 but the contact caused **no damage or injury**.

tiles.name: Compelled
tiles.note: Blue pushes you onto the mark

blocks.p: An exonerated boat takes no penalty. But the hearing finds the facts: if nobody forced you onto the mark, you are disqualified. And a right-of-way boat that could have avoided a collision with damage has broken rule 14 too.

sections.title: A yellow flag instead of turns

qa.q: How does the Scoring Penalty with a yellow flag work under rule 44.3?
qa.a: Where the notice of race or sailing instructions specify the **Scoring Penalty**, show a yellow flag at the first reasonable opportunity, keep it up until you finish and tell the race committee. It costs 20% of the DNF score.

blocks.p: Where the notice of race or sailing instructions specify the **Scoring Penalty** (rule 44.3), it replaces the turns: show a yellow flag at the first reasonable opportunity, keep it up until you finish, then tell the race committee and name the other boat. Otherwise a yellow flag is no penalty.
It costs 20% of the DNF score, rounded to a tenth of a point (or the points stated), never takes you beyond DNF and changes nobody else's score.

Where **Appendix T** applies, you may still take a 30% **Post-Race Penalty** in writing before the hearing begins. Neither is open to a boat that had to retire. A rule marked **[DP]** carries a discretionary penalty, possibly less than disqualification.

qa.q: Can I take penalty turns if I was over the line at the start?
qa.a: No: turns do not cure being over the line. You return and start, keeping clear of boats not returning, or are scored **OCS**; the triangle penalties under flags Z, U and black need no hearing.

blocks.p: Turns do not cure being over the line at the start: you return and start, keeping clear of boats that are not returning, or you are scored OCS. The preparatory flag prices the **last minute**.

head: Flag
Caught in the last minute
After a general recall
rows: Over the line: round an end

blocks.p: The **triangle** joins the ends of the line and the first mark. These penalties need no hearing. Under Z and black they lapse only if the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal, and a black-flagged boat that sails the restart cannot discard her disqualification.

sections.title: A yellow flag from the jury

qa.q: What happens if a judge shows me a yellow flag for pumping under Appendix P?
qa.a: Under **Appendix P** the first yellow flag means two turns, or DSQ without a hearing; the second, retire, or a DSQ that cannot be excluded; the third, retire and score DNE, or DNE in every race.

blocks.p: Under **Appendix P** judges afloat penalise rule 42 at once: a sound signal, a yellow flag pointed at you, your sail number hailed.
A postponement, general recall or abandonment cancels the penalty, but it still counts towards your total.
